visual_text: Red plates: what the study was
Men with advanced Alzheimer's disease in long-term care
10 days white, 10 days red, 10 days white
On red: about 25% more food, 84% more fluid (average)
8 of the 9 ate or drank more
A year later: strongly contrasting blue also worked; pale red and pale blue did not
Later study, blue plates, 18 people with dementia, many pale foods on the menu: no clear increase in eating
2026 review: 4 studies, 64 people, none randomised, longest 30 days. Evidence limited, low quality, inconclusive
Cheap to try. Keep helping at the meal.
Dunne et al., Clin Nutr 2004; Gaffney et al., Nutrients 2026
alt_text: Card 1 of 2. Red plates study: nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease in long-term care had 10 days on white plates, 10 on red, 10 on white. On red they ate about 25% more food and drank 84% more on average. Eight of the nine ate or drank more; one did not. Dunne 2004.

Card 2 of 2. What came after: a year later strong blue also worked, pale red and pale blue did not. A later blue plate study in 18 people with dementia, with many pale foods, showed no clear increase. A 2026 review: 4 small studies, 64 people, none randomised; evidence limited and inconclusive. Cheap to try; keep helping.
design_instructions: Carousel 2 cards, 1080x1350. Card 2: three mint bands with icons (blue and pale plates; blue plate with 18 person outlines; four documents), deep teal strip. Claims C13-33-a, C13-33-c, C13-33-d.
